    Calculate Multiple Diversity Indices

    Div.Rd

    Calculates a comprehensive set of diversity indices for benthic community data in a single function call, including alpha diversity, rarefaction, and beta diversity components.

    Div(DF, base = "ln", n, method = "hellinger", shape = "w", simpson = FALSE)

    Arguments

    DF

    A data.frame containing species abundance data. The first column should contain station names (if shape = "w") or species names (if shape = "l").

    base

    Logarithm base for Shannon calculation. Options are:

    • "ln" - Natural logarithm (default, most common in ecology)

    • "2" - Log base 2 (information theory)

    • "10" - Log base 10

    See Shannon for details.

    n

    Integer. Sample size for rarefaction. Must be less than or equal to the smallest total abundance across stations. See Esn for details.

    method

    Dissimilarity method for beta diversity (LCBD) calculation. Default is "hellinger". See BetaDiv for available methods.

    shape

    Data format specification (default = "w"):

    • "w" - Wide format: stations in rows, species in columns (first column = station names) (default)

    • "l" - Long format: species in rows, stations in columns (first column = species names)

    simpson

    Logical. Should Simpson's diversity index (1-lambda) be included? Default is FALSE. Set to TRUE to include Simpson diversity in the output.

    Value

    A data.frame with one row per station and the following columns:

    • Stations - Station or sample names

    • N - Total abundance (number of individuals)

    • Richness - Number of species (S)

    • Esn - Expected species richness at standardized sample size (rarefaction)

    • Shannon - Shannon diversity index (H')

    • Hmax - Maximum possible Shannon diversity

    • J - Pielou's evenness index (J')

    • Dominance - Simpson's dominance index (lambda)

    • Simpson - Simpson's diversity index (1-lambda) (only if simpson = TRUE)

    • LCBD - Local contribution to beta diversity

    • pLCBD - P-value for LCBD (from permutation test)

    • adpLCBD - Adjusted p-value for LCBD (Holm correction)

    Details

    This function is a convenient wrapper that calculates multiple diversity indices in a single call, providing a comprehensive characterization of benthic community diversity at each station. It combines:

    Alpha diversity metrics:

    • Abundance (N) - Total number of individuals

    • Richness (S) - Number of species present

    • Rarefied richness (Esn) - Expected species richness standardized to sample size n, allowing fair comparison across samples with different sampling efforts

    • Shannon diversity (H') - Accounts for both richness and evenness, incorporating the proportional abundance of each species

    • Maximum diversity (Hmax) - Theoretical maximum Shannon diversity if all species were equally abundant

    • Evenness (J') - Pielou's index measuring how evenly individuals are distributed among species (H'/Hmax)

    • Dominance (lambda) - Simpson's dominance index, the probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to the same species

    • Simpson (1-lambda) - Simpson's diversity index, the probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to different species (optional)

    Beta diversity metric:

    • LCBD - Local Contribution to Beta Diversity, measuring how compositionally unique each station is compared to the overall dataset

    All individual functions are called internally with the specified parameters. Error handling ensures that if one index fails to calculate, others will still be returned with NA values for the failed index.

    This comprehensive approach is particularly useful for:

    • Routine diversity assessments

    • Comparative studies across multiple stations

    • Environmental impact assessments

    • Monitoring programs

    • Ecological status evaluations

    References

    Magurran, A.E. (2004). Measuring Biological Diversity. Blackwell Publishing.

    Gray, J.S. & Elliott, M. (2009). Ecology of Marine Sediments: From Science to Management (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press, New York. 225 pp.

    Legendre, P. & De Caceres, M. (2013). Beta diversity as the variance of community data: dissimilarity coefficients and partitioning. Ecology Letters, 16(8), 951-963. https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.12141

    Shannon, C.E. & Weaver, W. (1949). The Mathematical Theory of Communication. University of Illinois Press.

    Simpson, E.H. (1949). Measurement of diversity. Nature, 163, 688. https://doi.org/10.1038/163688a0

    See also

    Shannon, Richness, Esn, Pielou, Dominance, Simpson, BetaDiv

    Examples

    # Example 1: Calculate all diversity indices (default, no Simpson)
data_wide <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St1", "St2", "St3"),
  Capitella = c(45, 12, 3),
  Owenia = c(23, 18, 45),
  Nephtys = c(12, 34, 23),
  Lumbrineris = c(8, 15, 12)
)

# Calculate all indices (rarefy to n=60, natural log for Shannon)
diversity_results <- Div(data_wide, base = "ln", n = 60,
                         method = "hellinger", shape = "w")
diversity_results
#>   Stations  N Richness Esn  Shannon     Hmax         J Dominance      LCBD
#> 1      St1 88        4   4 1.183353 1.386294 0.8536086 0.3566632 0.4832115
#> 2      St2 79        4   4 1.301567 1.386294 0.9388822 0.2962666 0.1499617
#> 3      St3 83        4   4 1.087143 1.386294 0.7842080 0.3929453 0.3668268
#>   pLCBD adpLCBD
#> 1 0.263   0.789
#> 2 0.781   1.000
#> 3 0.500   1.000

# Example 2: Include Simpson diversity index
Div(data_wide, base = "ln", n = 60, method = "hellinger",
    shape = "w", simpson = TRUE)
#>   Stations  N Richness Esn  Shannon     Hmax         J Dominance   Simpson
#> 1      St1 88        4   4 1.183353 1.386294 0.8536086 0.3566632 0.6433368
#> 2      St2 79        4   4 1.301567 1.386294 0.9388822 0.2962666 0.7037334
#> 3      St3 83        4   4 1.087143 1.386294 0.7842080 0.3929453 0.6070547
#>        LCBD pLCBD adpLCBD
#> 1 0.4832115 0.232   0.696
#> 2 0.1499617 0.800   0.958
#> 3 0.3668268 0.479   0.958

# Example 3: Using log base 2 for Shannon
Div(data_wide, base = "2", n = 60, method = "hellinger", shape = "w")
#>   Stations  N Richness Esn  Shannon     Hmax        J Dominance      LCBD pLCBD
#> 1      St1 88        4   4 1.707217 1.386294 1.231497 0.3566632 0.4832115 0.237
#> 2      St2 79        4   4 1.877764 1.386294 1.354521 0.2962666 0.1499617 0.780
#> 3      St3 83        4   4 1.568416 1.386294 1.131373 0.3929453 0.3668268 0.507
#>   adpLCBD
#> 1   0.711
#> 2   1.000
#> 3   1.000

# Example 4: Using chord transformation for beta diversity
Div(data_wide, base = "ln", n = 60, method = "chord", shape = "w")
#>   Stations  N Richness Esn  Shannon     Hmax         J Dominance      LCBD
#> 1      St1 88        4   4 1.183353 1.386294 0.8536086 0.3566632 0.4693053
#> 2      St2 79        4   4 1.301567 1.386294 0.9388822 0.2962666 0.2181004
#> 3      St3 83        4   4 1.087143 1.386294 0.7842080 0.3929453 0.3125943
#>   pLCBD adpLCBD
#> 1 0.248   0.744
#> 2 0.754   1.000
#> 3 0.562   1.000

# Example 5: Long format data
data_long <- data.frame(
  Species = c("Capitella", "Owenia", "Nephtys"),
  St1 = c(45, 23, 12),
  St2 = c(12, 18, 34),
  St3 = c(3, 45, 23)
)
Div(data_long, base = "ln", n = 50, method = "hellinger", shape = "l")
#>   Stations  N Richness Esn   Shannon     Hmax         J Dominance      LCBD
#> 1      St1 80        3   3 0.9665884 1.098612 0.8798267 0.4215625 0.4726228
#> 2      St2 64        3   3 1.0066670 1.098612 0.9163078 0.3964844 0.1456841
#> 3      St3 71        3   3 0.7878628 1.098612 0.7171436 0.5084309 0.3816932
#>   pLCBD adpLCBD
#> 1 0.292   0.876
#> 2 0.790   0.890
#> 3 0.445   0.890
